![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14083756/assets/517276d5122f1a81b894da7be7796c5941a16442987f99f476220979bc5688c7.png)

The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(3,2.6)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ The point $B$ has coordinates $(2.6,3)$ and lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ If ${f}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{3},$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2.6)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $B\,(2.6,3)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(2.6)=3.$
We're also told that ${f}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{3}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=2.6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(2.6) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2.6))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
